sections.title: Define the SEO fix before you verify it
sections.body: A verification plan starts with a precise statement of the problem and intended change. “Improve SEO” is too broad to test. “The canonical on these product pages should point to the preferred indexable URL” is specific enough to inspect. Write the affected URLs, the current condition, the intended condition, the owner, the release dependency and the reason for the change. Record the before state before editing anything. Depending on the fix, that may include source HTML, rendered output, HTTP headers, crawl observations, indexation status, page content, internal links, Search Console rows or an analytics baseline. Keep the capture dated and reproducible. This is not bureaucracy. Without a baseline, a later state has no comparison. Without a precise intended state, a team can declare a ticket complete while the underlying issue remains. The initial brief should also state what the fix is not expected to change. That boundary helps avoid treating unrelated ranking movement as proof.

sections.title: Verify the SEO fix reached the live site
sections.body: The first after-check is implementation verification. Inspect the production URL, not only a branch, staging environment or ticket description. Confirm the relevant HTML, headers, structured data, robots directive, canonical, redirect, internal link, title, description or content block is present as intended. Check the response and rendered state when JavaScript or a template can alter what users and crawlers receive. Test more than one URL when the fix uses a shared template, but keep the sample tied to the stated scope. Confirm that the release did not introduce a redirect loop, blocked response, broken link or unexpected noindex. If the live state is wrong, stop there: search performance cannot validate an implementation that never shipped correctly. Record the URL, timestamp and observation. A clean ticket is not a live check. A screenshot without the URL and date is weak evidence. The goal is a small, auditable record that shows the intended change exists where search users and crawlers can encounter it.

sections.title: Compare before and after SEO evidence
sections.body: The comparison should use the same definition, scope and source wherever possible. If the issue was a missing title, compare the prior and current title on the affected pages. If it was indexation, inspect the relevant coverage or inspection state after allowing for processing time. If it was internal linking, compare the link relationship and crawl access rather than only page views. Preserve the original baseline; do not replace it with a new export. Where a direct comparison is impossible, explain the difference. Search data often has latency and noise. Use a realistic observation window and avoid selecting only a favourable day. For a content change, compare the target query and page signals with an appropriate pre-period, while noting other changes that occurred. For a technical change, the first proof may be a correct live response and later crawl observation, not an immediate ranking increase. “Before and after” describes a method of comparison, not a promise that every metric moves upward. It is valid to conclude that implementation is correct, outcome evidence is not yet available, or the hypothesis needs revision.

sections.title: What counts as proof of an SEO fix
sections.body: Proof depends on the claim. For an implementation claim, production inspection showing the intended state is the primary proof. For a crawl or indexation claim, relevant crawler or inspection evidence matters. For a search outcome claim, use a suitable baseline, date range and query or page segmentation, then acknowledge competing changes and lag. For a business outcome claim, connect the page or query to the agreed event without implying causation the data cannot establish. A single screenshot, rank observation or tool score rarely proves a broad outcome. Strong evidence is specific, dated and proportionate. It lets another person reproduce the check or understand why reproduction is currently impossible. It also records negative results. If the state did not change, if crawlers have not revisited it, or if the signal is inconclusive, say that plainly. That is not failure of the process; it is a useful decision point. The next action might be a release correction, a longer observation window, a narrower hypothesis or no further work. Verification protects the team from both false confidence and endless testing.

sections.title: Create a reusable SEO fix verification record
sections.body: Keep the record short enough that it will be maintained. Include the issue, affected URLs, baseline source and date, intended change, release date, implementation result, observation window, outcome evidence, limitations and next action. Link to the relevant ticket or deployment where available. Name the person who performed the check and the source they used. If several changes landed together, state that attribution is limited. If the fix was rolled back, record the rollback state rather than leaving the task marked complete. The record should serve the next reviewer, not only the person who did the work. This is particularly important for agencies, distributed teams and migrations where context can be lost between recommendation and release. A consistent record also improves future prioritisation: repeated failures may reveal a template or process problem rather than isolated page issues. The point of verifying an SEO fix is not to produce another report. It is to make the next decision safer and more informed.

sections.title: When an SEO fix does not produce the expected result
sections.body: Return to the verification layers in order. First, confirm the intended state still exists in production and across the stated scope. Releases, templates and content systems can overwrite a correct change. Next, confirm that crawlers can reach and process the state and that enough time has passed for the relevant source to update. Then revisit the original reasoning. The issue may have had another cause, the action may have addressed only part of it, or other site and market changes may dominate the signal. Do not keep repeating the same implementation because the expected outcome was absent. Record the negative result and choose whether to correct, investigate, monitor or stop. A failed hypothesis can save future work when documented. It shows which evidence was insufficient and which check should improve next time. The goal is not to defend the recommendation. It is to reach a better next decision without erasing the history that led there.

sections.title: Avoid weak proof when you verify an SEO fix
sections.body: Do not use a single rank check to prove a broad change, because location, device, personalisation and normal result movement can alter the observation. Do not compare different page groups or date definitions without stating the difference. Do not treat an automated audit score as proof that the intended production state exists. Do not wait for traffic when the fix can already be checked directly in HTML or headers. Avoid changing the baseline after seeing the outcome, and avoid selecting only the queries or days that support the preferred story. These errors are usually process problems rather than bad intent. A written check established before release makes them less likely. When the available source is imperfect, label the limitation and narrow the claim. Useful proof is proportionate to the decision. A low-risk metadata correction needs a lighter record than a migration, but both need a clear before state, intended state and reviewer.

steps: State the intended SEO change, affected URLs, exclusions and capture the dated before state.
Inspect production rather than staging or the ticket to confirm the intended change was implemented.
Compare the same source and scope before and after, allowing for crawler, processing and reporting lag.
Match proof to the claim: implementation, crawl, search or business outcome need different evidence.
Record limitations, competing changes, the reviewer and the next action so another person can repeat the check.
